problems.problem: When the numbers $A$ and $B$ are expanded into infinite decimal fractions, the lengths of the minimal periods of these fractions are $6$ and $12$ respectively. What can the length of the minimal period of the number $A+B$ be?

The grandfather of Baron K. F. I. von Münchhausen built a square castle, divided it into $9$ equal square halls and placed the arsenal in the central one. The Baron's father divided each of the $8$ remaining halls into $9$ equal square chambers and set up winter gardens in all the central chambers. The Baron himself divided each of the $64$ free chambers into $9$ equal square rooms, set up a swimming pool in each of the central rooms and made the rest living rooms.

The Baron boasts that he managed to walk through all the living rooms, visiting each exactly once, and to return to the initial one (in each wall between two adjacent living rooms there is a door). Can the Baron's words be true?

From any point on either of the two banks of a river one can swim to the other bank covering at most one kilometre. Can a pilot always steer a ship along the river so as to stay all the time at a distance of at most a) $700$ metres; b) $800$ metres from each of the banks?

Note. It is known that the river connects two round lakes of radius $10$ kilometres each, and that the bank lines consist of segments and arcs of circles. The ship is to be regarded as a point.

For every pair of real numbers $a$ and $b$ consider the sequence of numbers $p_n=[2\{an+b\}]$. Any $k$ consecutive terms of this sequence are called a word. Is it true that every ordered collection of zeros and ones of length $k$ is a word of the sequence defined by some $a$ and $b$

a) for $k=4$;

b) for $k=5$?

Note: $[c]$ is the integer part and $\{c\}$ the fractional part of the number $c$.

In a botanical identification guide plants are described by a hundred features. Each feature may be either present or absent. The guide is called good if any two plants differ in more than half of the features. Prove that a good guide cannot describe more than $50$ plants.

A square with centre $O$ is constructed externally on the side $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AC$ and $BC$ respectively, and the lengths of these sides are $a$ and $b$ respectively. Find the maximum of the sum $OM+ON$ as the angle $ACB$ varies.
A pupil did not notice the multiplication sign between two seven-digit numbers and wrote one fourteen-digit number, which turned out to be three times their product. Find these numbers.

An infinite sequence of numbers $x_n$ is defined by the conditions $x_{n+1}=1-|1-2x_n|$, with $0\leqslant x_1\leqslant 1$. Prove that the sequence is periodic from some term onwards a) if and b) only if $x_1$ is rational.

Each of the $1994$ deputies of a parliament slapped exactly one of his colleagues in the face. Prove that a parliamentary commission of $665$ people can be formed whose members have not settled accounts with each other in the way indicated above.

$D$ is a point on the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Circles are inscribed in the triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, and their common external tangent (other than $BC$) is drawn, meeting $AD$ at the point $K$. Prove that the length of the segment $AK$ does not depend on the position of the point $D$ on $BC$.

An arbitrary polygon (not necessarily convex) is considered.

a) Is there always a chord of the polygon that divides it into parts of equal area?

b) Prove that any polygon can be divided by some chord into parts each of which has area at least $1/3$ of the area of the polygon.

(A chord of a polygon is a segment whose endpoints belong to the boundary of the polygon and which lies entirely in the polygon, boundary included.)
Is there a polynomial $P(x)$ that has a negative coefficient while all the coefficients of every power $P^n(x)$, $n>1$, of it are positive?

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. For an arbitrary point $P$ inside the triangle, consider the points $A'$ and $C'$ in which the lines $AP$ and $CP$ meet $BC$ and $BA$ respectively. Find the locus of points $P$ for which the segments $AA'$ and $CC'$ are equal.

The diagonals of a trapezoid $ABCD$ meet at the point $K$. Circles are constructed on the lateral sides of the trapezoid as diameters. The point $K$ lies outside these circles. Prove that the lengths of the tangents drawn to these circles from the point $K$ are equal.

Initially four identical right triangles are given. At each move one of the existing triangles is cut along the altitude (issuing from the right angle) into two others. Is it true that after any number of moves there will be two identical triangles among the triangles?
Integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that the numbers $\dfrac{a}{b}+\dfrac{b}{c}+\dfrac{c}{a}$ and $\dfrac{a}{c}+\dfrac{c}{b}+\dfrac{b}{a}$ are also integers. Prove that $|a|=|b|=|c|$.

Several light bulbs are lit on a board. There are several buttons. Pressing a button changes the state of the bulbs connected to it. It is known that for every set of bulbs there is a button connected to an odd number of bulbs of this set. Prove that by pressing buttons one can switch off all the bulbs.
Positive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $a^2+b^2-ab=c^2$. Prove that $(a-c)(b-c)\leqslant 0$.

In a $10\times 10$ squared square the centres of all unit squares are marked ($100$ points in all). What is the smallest number of lines, not parallel to the sides of the square, that must be drawn to cross out all the marked points?

The points $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_{n-1}$ divide the side $BC$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ into $n$ equal parts: $BP_1=P_1P_2=\ldots=P_{n-1}C$. A point $M$ is chosen on the side $AC$ so that $AM=BP_1$. Prove that $\angle AP_1M+\angle AP_2M+\ldots+\angle AP_{n-1}M=30^\circ$ if a) $n=3$; b) $n$ is an arbitrary natural number (see the figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_1996_0_p3_fig.png

A rook stands in a corner of an $m\times n$ chessboard. Two players in turn move it vertically or horizontally by any number of squares; it is not allowed for the rook to stop on or pass through a square on which it has already been (or through which it has already passed). The player who has no move loses. Which of the players can secure a win: the first player or his partner, and how should he play?

In a country whose inhabitants' houses are points of the plane, two laws are in force:

1) A person may play basketball only if he is taller than the majority of his neighbours.

2) A person is entitled to free public transport only if he is shorter than the majority of his neighbours.

In each law the neighbours of a person are all the people living in a disc of some radius centred at this person's house. Each person chooses the radius for the first law himself, and the radius (not necessarily the same) for the second law. Can at least $90\%$ of the people of this country play basketball and at least $90\%$ of the people be entitled to free transport?

Prove that for every polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n$ with natural coefficients there is an integer $k$ such that the numbers $P(k), P(k+1), \ldots, P(k+1996)$ are all composite, if a) $n=1$; b) $n$ is an arbitrary natural number.
Is there a convex body other than a ball whose orthogonal projections onto three pairwise perpendicular planes are all discs?
Prove that among the quadrilaterals with given lengths of the diagonals and given angle between them, the parallelogram has the smallest perimeter.

a) Each side of a quadrilateral, traversed clockwise, was extended beyond its end by its own length. It turned out that the endpoints of the constructed segments are the vertices of a square. Prove that the original quadrilateral is a square.

b) Prove that if the same procedure applied to an $n$-gon yields a regular $n$-gon, then the original $n$-gon is regular.

Real numbers $a_1\leqslant a_2\leqslant a_3$ and $b_1\leqslant b_2\leqslant b_3$ are given such that $a_1+a_2+a_3=b_1+b_2+b_3$ and $a_1a_2+a_2a_3+a_1a_3=b_1b_2+b_2b_3+b_1b_3$. Prove that if $a_1\leqslant b_1$, then $a_3\leqslant b_3$.

In a round-robin tournament there were no draws; a win gave $1$ point and a loss $0$. Then the coefficient of each participant was determined: it was equal to the sum of the points scored by those whom this sportsman defeated. It turned out that all participants had the same coefficient. The number of participants of the tournament is greater than two. Prove that all the sportsmen scored the same number of points.

Consider the sequence of first digits of the powers of five: $1, 5, 2, 1, 6, \ldots$. Prove that any block of this sequence, written in reverse order, occurs in the sequence of first digits of the powers of two ($1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 3, \ldots$).
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-negative integers such that $28a+30b+31c=365$. Prove that $a+b+c=12$.
A square with side $1$ is cut into rectangles, and one side of each of them is marked. Prove that the sum of the lengths of all the marked sides cannot be less than $1$.

A road of length $1$ km is completely lit by street lamps, each lamp lighting a segment of the road of length $1$ m. What is the largest number of lamps there can be on the road if it is known that after switching off any lamp the road will no longer be completely lit?
Is there a natural number divisible by $1998$ whose sum of digits is less than $27$?

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ cut out of plywood is laid on the floor. Three nails are driven into the floor (one close against each side of the triangle) so that the triangle cannot be rotated without lifting it off the floor. The first nail divides the side $AB$ in the ratio $1:3$ counting from the vertex $A$, the second divides the side $BC$ in the ratio $2:1$ counting from the vertex $B$. In what ratio does the third nail divide the side $AC$?

The natural numbers from $1$ to $n$ are arranged in a row in an arbitrary order (the number $n$ is fixed). An arrangement is called bad if one can mark in it $10$ numbers (not necessarily standing consecutively) going in decreasing order. The other arrangements are called good. Prove that the number of good arrangements does not exceed $81^n$.
It is known that $(a+b+c)c<0$. Prove that $b^2>4ac$.

Two circles intersect at the points $P$ and $Q$. A third circle with centre at the point $P$ meets the first circle at the points $A$, $B$, and the second at the points $C$ and $D$ (see the figure). Prove that the angles $AQD$ and $BQC$ are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_1999_0_p2_fig.png
Find all pairs of natural numbers $x$, $y$ such that the numbers $x^3+y$ and $y^3+x$ are divisible by $x^2+y^2$.

$2n$ radii divide a disc into $2n$ equal sectors: $n$ blue and $n$ red. In the blue sectors, starting from some one, the numbers from $1$ to $n$ are written in a row counterclockwise. In the red sectors, starting from some one, the same numbers are written in the same way, but clockwise. Prove that there is a half-disc in which all the numbers from $1$ to $n$ are written.

A grasshopper jumps on the segment $[0,1]$. In one jump it can get from a point $x$ either to the point $x/\sqrt3$ or to the point $x/\sqrt3+(1-1/\sqrt3)$. A point $a$ is chosen on the segment $[0,1]$. Prove that, starting from any point, the grasshopper can after several jumps be at a distance less than $1/100$ from the point $a$.

For the numbers $1, \ldots, 1999$ placed around a circle, the sum of the products of all sets of $10$ consecutive numbers is computed. Find an arrangement of the numbers for which the resulting sum is the largest.

Points $A$ and $B$ are taken on the graph of the function $y=1/x$, $x>0$. Perpendiculars are dropped from them to the abscissa axis; the feet of the perpendiculars are $H_A$ and $H_B$; $O$ is the origin. Prove that the area of the figure bounded by the lines $OA$, $OB$ and the arc $AB$ equals the area of the figure bounded by the lines $AH_A$, $BH_B$, the abscissa axis and the arc $AB$.

Let $f(x)=x^2+12x+30$. Solve the equation
$$f(f(f(f(f(x)))))=0.$$

A convex polygon is drawn on squared paper so that all its vertices are at vertices of the squares and none of its sides is vertical or horizontal. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the vertical segments of grid lines contained inside the polygon equals the sum of the lengths of the horizontal segments of grid lines inside the polygon.

$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral. The circles constructed on the segments $AB$ and $CD$ as diameters touch each other externally at a point $M$ different from the intersection point of the diagonals of the quadrilateral. The circle passing through the points $A$, $M$ and $C$ meets for the second time the line joining the point $M$ and the midpoint of $AB$ at the point $K$, and the circle passing through the points $B$, $M$ and $D$ meets the same line for the second time at the point $L$. Prove that $|MK-ML|=|AB-CD|$.

A sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, \ldots$ will be denoted by $\{x_n\}$. From available sequences $\{b_n\}$ and $\{c_n\}$ (possibly $\{b_n\}$ coincides with $\{c_n\}$) one is allowed to obtain the sequences $\{b_n+c_n\}$, $\{b_n-c_n\}$, $\{b_n\cdot c_n\}$ and $\left\{\dfrac{b_n}{c_n}\right\}$ (if all $c_n$ are non-zero). Besides, from any available sequence one can obtain a new one by deleting several initial terms. At first only the sequence $\{a_n\}$ is available. Can one obtain from it by the operations described above the sequence $\{n\}$, that is, $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots$, if a) $a_n=n^2$; b) $a_n=n+\sqrt2$; c) $a_n=\dfrac{n^{2000}+1}{n}$?

$7$ cards were taken out of a deck, shown to everybody, shuffled, and Grisha and Lyosha were dealt $3$ cards each, while the remaining card was a) hidden; b) given to Kolya. Grisha and Lyosha may in turn announce aloud any information about their cards. Can they tell each other their cards in such a way that Kolya cannot work out the location of any of the cards he does not see? (Grisha and Lyosha did not agree on any special way of communicating; all negotiations are conducted openly.)
Do there exist three quadratic trinomials such that each of them has a root, while the sum of any two of the trinomials has no roots?
Can guards be placed around a point object so that it is impossible to approach either the object or the sentries unnoticed? (Each sentry stands motionless and sees $100$ m strictly forward.)

Give an example of a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $2001$ for which the identity
$$P(x)+P(1-x)=1$$
holds.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AH_A$, $BH_B$ and $CH_C$ are drawn. Prove that the triangle with vertices at the orthocentres of the triangles $AH_BH_C$, $BH_AH_C$, $CH_AH_B$ is congruent to the triangle $H_AH_BH_C$.

A black and a white counter stand on two squares of a chessboard. In one move one may move either of them to an adjacent square vertically or horizontally (two counters cannot stand on one square). Can all possible arrangements of these two counters occur as a result of such moves, each exactly once?

In the game "Landing Force" two armies are conquering a country. They move in turn, each move occupying one of the free cities. An army captures its first city from the air, and with each subsequent move it may capture any city connected by a road with some city already occupied by this army. If there are no such cities, the army stops military operations (the other army may possibly continue its actions). Is there a scheme of cities and roads such that the army moving second can capture more than half of all the cities, no matter how the first army acts? (The number of cities is finite, each road connects exactly two cities.)
problems.proposer: P. Grozman, A. Shapovalov, D. Shapovalov

problems.problem: The tangents of the angles of a triangle are natural numbers. What can these numbers be equal to?
It is known about positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ that $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\geqslant a+b+c$. Prove that $a+b+c\geqslant 3abc$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the points $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $CD$ respectively. The segments $AE$, $AF$ and $EF$ divide the quadrilateral into $4$ triangles whose areas are equal to consecutive natural numbers. What is the largest possible value of the area of the triangle $ABD$?

Every spectator who bought a ticket for the first row of a cinema took one of the seats in the first row. It turned out that all the seats in the first row were taken, but every spectator was sitting in a seat other than his own. The usher may interchange neighbours if both are sitting in seats other than their own. Can he always seat everybody in their own seats?

In the town of Udoev the mayor is elected as follows. If in the current round of voting none of the candidates has received more than half of the votes, the next round is held with all the candidates except the last one by number of votes. (Two candidates never get equal numbers of votes; if a candidate gets more than half of the votes, he becomes mayor and the election ends.) In each round each voter votes for one of the candidates. If this candidate has gone through to the next round, the voter votes for him again. If the candidate has dropped out, then all his voters vote for one and the same candidate from among those remaining.

At the latest election $2002$ candidates stood. Ostap Bender, who took the $k$-th place by number of votes in the first round, became mayor. Determine the largest possible value of $k$ if Ostap was elected

a) in the $1002$-nd round;

b) in the $1001$-st round.

Can all the points of a square and of a disc be coloured black and white so that the sets of white points of these figures are similar to each other and the sets of black points are also similar to each other (possibly with different ratios of similarity)?
Are there natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that each of the equations $ax^2+bx+c=0$, $ax^2+bx-c=0$, $ax^2-bx+c=0$, $ax^2-bx-c=0$ has both roots integers?

A closed broken line passing through every vertex exactly once is drawn along the edges of a convex polyhedron with $2003$ vertices. Prove that in each of the parts into which this broken line divides the surface of the polyhedron, the number of faces with an odd number of sides is odd.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with leading coefficient $1$, and let $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ be a sequence of integers such that $P(a_1)=0$, $P(a_2)=a_1$, $P(a_3)=a_2$, and so on. The numbers in the sequence do not repeat. What degree can $P(x)$ have?

Let $M$ be the intersection point of the medians of $\triangle ABC$. On the perpendiculars dropped from $M$ to the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$, points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively are taken, with $A_1B_1\perp MC$ and $A_1C_1\perp MB$. Prove that $M$ is also the intersection point of the medians of $\triangle A_1B_1C_1$.

A country has several cities connected by one-way and two-way roads. It is known that from every city one can travel to any other one by exactly one path not passing twice through the same city. Prove that the country can be divided into three provinces so that no road connects two cities of the same province.
problems.proposer: A. V. Spivak, I. V. Mezhirov

problems.problem: An infinite sequence of polynomials $P_1(x), P_2(x), \ldots$ is given. Is there always a finite set of functions $f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_N(x)$ by compositions of which any of them can be written (for example, $P_1(x)=f_2(f_1(f_2(x)))$)?
An arithmetic progression consists of integers. The sum of the first $n$ terms of this progression is a power of two. Prove that $n$ is also a power of two.
Is there a tetrahedron all of whose faces are congruent right triangles?

Call white the numbers of the form $\sqrt{a+b\sqrt2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are non-zero integers. Similarly, call black the numbers of the form $\sqrt{c+d\sqrt7}$, where $c$ and $d$ are non-zero integers. Can a black number be equal to a sum of several white ones?

Call a natural number allowed if it has at most $20$ distinct prime divisors. Initially there is a pile of $2004!$ (that is, $1\cdot2\cdot\ldots\cdot2004$) stones. Two players in turn take from the pile some allowed number of stones (possibly a new one each time). The player who takes the last stones wins. Who wins with correct play?

The radius of the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$ equals the radius of the circle touching the side $AB$ at the point $C'$ and the extensions of the other two sides at the points $A'$ and $B'$. Prove that the centre of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ coincides with the orthocentre (the intersection point of the altitudes) of the triangle $A'B'C'$.

A deck of $36$ cards lies face down in front of a psychic ($4$ suits, nine cards of each suit). He names the suit of the top card, after which the card is turned over and shown to him. After that the psychic names the suit of the next card, and so on. The psychic's task is to guess the suit as many times as possible.

The backs of the cards are asymmetric, and the psychic sees in which of two positions the top card lies. The psychic's assistant knows the order of the cards in the deck and cannot change it, but he can place the back of each card in one way or the other.

Could the psychic make an agreement with his assistant, while the latter did not yet know the order of the cards, ensuring that the suit is guessed for at least a) $19$ cards; b) $23$ cards?

If you have devised a way of guessing some other number of cards greater than $19$, write it down too.
Is there a plane quadrilateral in which the tangents of all the interior angles are equal?

Two points with integer coordinates are marked on the graph of a polynomial with integer coefficients. Prove that if the distance between them is an integer, then the segment joining them is parallel to the abscissa axis.

Squares $ABB_1A_2$, $BCC_1B_2$ and $CAA_1C_2$ are constructed externally on the sides of a triangle $ABC$. On the segments $A_1A_2$ and $B_1B_2$, squares $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ and $B_1B_2B_3B_4$ are also constructed, outwards from $\triangle AA_1A_2$ and $\triangle BB_1B_2$. Prove that $A_3B_4\parallel AB$.

A construction set consists of a collection of rectangular parallelepipeds. All of them can be placed in one box, which also has the form of a rectangular parallelepiped. In a defective set one of the dimensions of each parallelepiped turned out to be smaller than the standard one. Can one always also decrease one of the dimensions of the box into which the set is packed (the parallelepipeds are packed into the box so that their edges are parallel to the edges of the box)?
The sequence $a_n=1+2^n+\ldots+5^n$ is given. Are there $5$ consecutive terms of it divisible by $2005$?

$200$ points are given in space. Every two of them are joined by a segment, and the segments do not intersect each other. The first player colours each segment in one of $k$ colours, and then the second player colours each point in one of the same colours. If there are two points and the segment between them all coloured in one colour, the first player wins; otherwise the second one wins. Prove that the first player can guarantee himself a win if a) $k=7$; b) $k=10$.

One of two monic quadratic trinomials has two roots smaller than a thousand, and the other has two roots greater than a thousand. Can the sum of these trinomials have one root smaller than a thousand and the other greater than a thousand?
Can the sum of the tangents of the angles of one triangle be equal to the sum of the tangents of the angles of another one, if one of these triangles is acute-angled and the other obtuse-angled?
Can the whole space be tiled with congruent tetrahedra all of whose faces are right triangles?

A box contains cards numbered with the natural numbers from $1$ to $2006$. On the card with number $2006$ lies the card with number $2005$, and so on down to $1$. In one move one may take one top card (from any box) and put it either on the bottom of an empty box or on the card with the number one greater. How many empty boxes are needed in order to move all the cards into another box?
A natural number $n$ is such that the numbers $3n+1$ and $10n+1$ are squares of natural numbers. Prove that the number $29n+11$ is composite.

A triangle $ABC$ and points $P$ and $Q$ lying on its circumcircle are given. The point $P$ was reflected in the line $BC$, giving the point $P_a$. The intersection point of the lines $QP_a$ and $BC$ is denoted by $A'$. The points $B'$ and $C'$ are constructed similarly. Prove that the points $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ lie on one line.

Points $K$, $L$, $M$ and $N$ are marked on the sides of a unit square so that the line $KM$ is parallel to two sides of the square and the line $LN$ to the other two sides. The segment $KL$ cuts off from the square a triangle of perimeter $1$. What is the area of the triangle cut off from the square by the segment $MN$?

Can the $15$ segments shown in the figure be coloured in $3$ colours so that no $2$ segments of the same colour have a common endpoint?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_2007_0_p2_fig.png
Are there natural numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $x^2+x+1$ is a natural power of $y$, and $y^2+y+1$ is a natural power of $x$?

In his cabin Captain Vrungel is playing patience. A shuffled deck of $52$ cards is laid out in a circle; one place is free. The sailor Fuchs, without leaving the helm and without knowing the initial layout, names a card. If this card lies next to the free place, Vrungel moves it to this place without telling Fuchs. Otherwise nothing happens. Then Fuchs names another card, Vrungel performs the same action, and so on, as many times as he likes, until Fuchs says "enough". Fuchs wins if he says "enough" at a moment when every card is not in the place where it was at the beginning. Can Fuchs win for certain?

A triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. $X$ is an arbitrary point inside the triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle XAB=\angle XBC=\varphi$, and $P$ is a point such that $PX\perp OX$, $\angle XOP=\varphi$, the angles $\angle XOP$ and $\angle XAB$ having the same orientation. Prove that all such points $P$ lie on one line.

With a non-zero number one is allowed to perform the following operations: $x\mapsto\dfrac{1+x}{x}$, $x\mapsto\dfrac{1-x}{x}$. Is it true that from every non-zero rational number one can obtain every rational number by a finite number of such operations?

A lecture hall has the shape of a regular hexagon with side $3$ m. In each corner a snorometer is installed, which determines the number of sleeping students at a distance not exceeding $3$ m. How many sleeping students are there in the hall altogether if the sum of the readings of the snorometers equals $7$?

Andrei and Boris play the following game. Initially a robot stands on the number line at the point $p$. First Andrei names the distance by which the robot must move. Then Boris chooses the direction in which the robot moves by this distance. And so on. For which $p$ can Andrei achieve that in a finite number of moves the robot reaches one of the points $0$ or $1$ regardless of Boris's actions?

All the integers from $-33$ to $100$ inclusive were arranged in some order, and the sums of every two neighbouring numbers were considered. It turned out that there are no zeros among them. Then for each such sum its reciprocal was found. The numbers obtained were added. Could the result be an integer?
A certain polynomial with integer coefficients takes, at $k$ integer points, values among the numbers from $1$ to $k-1$. Prove that if $k\geqslant 6$, then these values are equal.

The altitudes $AA'$ and $CC'$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $H$. The point $B_0$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. Prove that the intersection point of the lines symmetric to $BB_0$ and $HB_0$ with respect to the bisectors of the angles $ABC$ and $AHC$ respectively lies on the line $A'C'$.

The natural numbers are coloured in $N$ colours. There are infinitely many numbers of each colour. It is known that the colour of the half-sum of two distinct numbers of the same parity depends only on the colours of the summands (for example, the half-sum of a blue and a red number is always yellow).

(a) Prove that the half-sum of numbers of the same parity and the same colour is always coloured in the same colour.

(b) For which $N$ is such a colouring possible?

Money can be transferred to a mobile phone through a payment terminal, and a commission, a whole positive number of percent, is charged. Fedya put a whole number of roubles into the terminal for his mobile phone, and his account was credited with $847$ roubles. How much money did Fedya put in, if it is known that the commission is less than $30\%$?

An increasing infinite sequence of natural numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n, \ldots$ is given such that each of its terms is either the arithmetic mean or the geometric mean of the two adjacent ones. Must this sequence from some moment on become either an arithmetic or a geometric progression?

A square is cut into a finite number of rectangles. Is there necessarily a segment joining the centres (the intersection points of the diagonals) of two rectangles that has no common points with any rectangles other than these two?

$2009$ beads are strung loosely on a ring. In one move any bead may be moved so that it is exactly in the middle between its two neighbours. Is there an initial arrangement of the beads and a sequence of moves in which some bead travels at least one full circle?

The sides $BC$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ touch the corresponding excircles at the points $A_1$, $B_1$. Let $A_2$, $B_2$ be the orthocentres of the triangles $CAA_1$ and $CBB_1$. Prove that the line $A_2B_2$ is perpendicular to the bisector of the angle $C$.

Prove that for any natural numbers $0<k<m<n$ the numbers $C_n^k$ and $C_n^m$ are not coprime. ($C_n^k=\dfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ is the number of ways to choose $k$ elements out of $n$ distinct elements without regard to order.)
It is known that the sum of any two of the three quadratic trinomials $x^2+ax+b$, $x^2+cx+d$, $x^2+ex+f$ has no roots. Can the sum of all these trinomials have roots?

A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD=a$ and $BC=b$ is given. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on the sides $AB$ and $CD$ respectively, and the segment $MN$ is parallel to the bases of the trapezoid. The diagonal $AC$ meets this segment at the point $O$. Find $MN$ if it is known that the areas of the triangles $AMO$ and $CNO$ are equal.

Is it possible, by applying to the number $2$ the functions $\sin$, $\cos$, $\operatorname{tg}$, $\operatorname{ctg}$, $\arcsin$, $\arccos$, $\operatorname{arctg}$, $\operatorname{arcctg}$ in any quantity and in any order, to obtain the number $2010$?
The sum of the digits of a number $n$ equals $100$. Can the sum of the digits of the number $n^3$ equal $100^3$?
In a scalene triangle two medians are equal to two altitudes. Find the ratio of the third median to the third altitude.

$4n$ points were marked in the plane, after which all pairs of points at distance $1$ cm from each other were joined by segments. It turned out that among any $n+1$ points there are necessarily two joined by a segment. Prove that at least $7n$ segments were drawn altogether.

Is there an arithmetic progression of $2011$ natural numbers in which the number of terms divisible by $8$ is less than the number of terms divisible by $9$, and the latter in turn is less than the number of terms divisible by $10$?

A $2010\times 2011$ board is covered by $2\times 1$ dominoes; some of them lie horizontally and some vertically. Prove that the boundary between the horizontal dominoes and the vertical ones has even length.
In a triangle $ABC$ the bisectors $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. It is known that the centre of the circumcircle of the triangle $BB_1C_1$ lies on the line $AC$. Find the angle $C$ of the triangle.

Vintik and Shpuntik each have three sticks of total length $1$ metre. Both Vintik and Shpuntik can form a triangle from their three sticks. At night Neznaika crept into their house, took one stick from Vintik and one from Shpuntik and interchanged them. In the morning it turned out that Vintik could not form a triangle from his sticks. Can one guarantee that Shpuntik can form one from his?

A cube is divided into rectangular parallelepipeds so that for any two of the parallelepipeds their projections onto some face of the cube overlap (that is, intersect in a figure of non-zero area). Prove that for any three of the parallelepipeds there is a face of the cube such that the projections of each two of them onto this face do not overlap.

Two firms in turn hire programmers, among whom there are $4$ geniuses. Each firm chooses its first programmer arbitrarily, and each subsequent one must be acquainted with someone hired earlier by that firm. If a firm cannot hire a programmer according to these rules, it stops hiring, while the other may continue. The list of programmers and their acquaintances is known in advance. Can the acquaintances be arranged so that the firm entering the game second can hire at least $3$ geniuses, no matter how the first firm acts?

Alyosha wrote on the board $5$ integers: the coefficients and the roots of a quadratic trinomial. Borya erased one of them. The numbers $2$, $3$, $4$, $-5$ remained, in some order. Recover the erased number and prove that it was exactly this number that was written.

Pluses and minuses stand in the cells of an $n\times n$ table. In one move one is allowed to change all the signs in an arbitrary row or in an arbitrary column to the opposite ones. It is known that from the initial arrangement one can obtain one in which all the cells contain pluses. Prove that this can be achieved in at most $n$ moves.
An equilateral triangle was cut out of the plane. Can the remaining part of the plane be tiled by triangles any two of which are similar but not homothetic?

An even number of pears are laid out in a circle. The masses of any two neighbouring ones differ by at most $1$ g. Prove that all the pears can be combined into pairs and laid out in a circle so that the masses of any two neighbouring pairs also differ by at most $1$ g.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. For an arbitrary line $l$ denote by $l_a$, $l_b$, $l_c$ the lines symmetric to $l$ with respect to the sides of the triangle, and by $I_l$ the centre of the incircle of the triangle formed by these lines. Find the locus of the points $I_l$.

Consider the graph whose vertices correspond to all possible three-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2^k\}$, and whose edges join the vertices corresponding to subsets that intersect in exactly one element. Find the smallest number of colours in which the vertices of the graph can be coloured so that any two vertices joined by an edge have different colours.

Two quadratic trinomials with leading coefficient $1$ are given. The graph of one of them meets the axis $Ox$ at the points $A$ and $M$, and the axis $Oy$ at the point $C$. The graph of the other meets the axis $Ox$ at the points $B$ and $M$, and the axis $Oy$ at the point $D$. (Here $O$ is the origin; the points are arranged as in the figure.) Prove that the triangles $AOC$ and $BOD$ are similar.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_2013_0_p1_fig.png

A boy and a girl were sitting on a long bench. Twenty more children came up to them one by one, and each of them sat down between some two of those already sitting. Call a girl brave if she sat down between two neighbouring boys, and a boy brave if he sat down between two neighbouring girls. When everybody was seated, it turned out that boys and girls were sitting alternately. How many of them were brave?
A regular $4n$-gon $A_1A_2\ldots A_{4n}$ of area $S$ is given, with $n>1$. Find the area of the quadrilateral $A_1A_nA_{n+1}A_{n+2}$.

A school decided to hold a table tennis tournament between the mathematics and the humanities classes. The humanities team consists of $n$ people and the mathematics team of $m$, with $n\ne m$. Since there is only one table, it was decided to play as follows. First some two pupils from different teams begin to play each other, and all the other participants line up in one common queue. After each game the person standing first in the queue replaces at the table the member of his own team, who goes to the end of the queue. Prove that sooner or later every mathematician will play with every humanities pupil.

A function $f(x)$ is given whose value at every integer $x$ is an integer. It is known that for every prime $p$ there is a polynomial $Q_p(x)$ of degree not exceeding $2013$ with integer coefficients such that $f(n)-Q_p(n)$ is divisible by $p$ for every integer $n$.

Is it true that there is a polynomial $g(x)$ with real coefficients such that $g(n)=f(n)$ for every integer $n$?

Let $I$ be the centre of the incircle of a scalene triangle $ABC$. Denote by $A_1$ the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ not containing the point $A$, and by $A_2$ the midpoint of the arc $BAC$. The perpendicular dropped from the point $A_1$ to the line $A_2I$ meets the line $BC$ at the point $A'$. The points $B'$ and $C'$ are defined similarly.

a) Prove that the points $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ lie on one line.

b) Prove that this line is perpendicular to the line $OI$, where $O$ is the centre of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.
The quadratic trinomial $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ takes values of different signs at the points $\dfrac1a$ and $c$. Prove that the roots of the trinomial $f(x)$ have different signs.

$21$ white and $21$ purple shirts hang in a row in a shop. Find the smallest $k$ such that for any initial order of the shirts one can take down $k$ white and $k$ purple shirts so that the remaining white shirts hang consecutively and the remaining purple shirts also hang consecutively.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. Denote by $M$ the midpoint of the side $AC$, and by $P$ the midpoint of the segment $CM$. The circumcircle of the triangle $ABP$ meets the segment $BC$ at an interior point $Q$. Prove that $\angle ABM=\angle MQP$.

Several white and several black points are given. From each white point an arrow goes to each black point, and a natural number is written on each arrow.

It is known that if one goes along any closed route, the product of the numbers on the arrows pointing in the direction of motion equals the product of the numbers on the arrows pointing against the direction of motion.

Is it then necessarily possible to put a natural number at each point so that the number on each arrow equals the product of the numbers at its endpoints?

A triangle with no equal angles is given. Petya and Vasya play the following game: in one move Petya marks a point in the plane, and Vasya colours it red or blue at his choice. Petya wins if some three of the points he has marked and Vasya has coloured form a monochromatic triangle similar to the original one.

In what smallest number of moves can Petya be sure to win (whatever the original triangle)?

A polynomial $P(x)$ has the following properties: $P(0)=1$, $(P(x))^2=1+x+x^{100}\cdot Q(x)$, where $Q(x)$ is some polynomial. Prove that the coefficient of $x^{99}$ in the polynomial $(P(x)+1)^{100}$ equals zero.

From an integer $a$ we construct the sequence
$$a_1=a,\quad a_2=1+a_1,\quad a_3=1+a_1a_2,\quad a_4=1+a_1a_2a_3,\quad \ldots$$
(each next number exceeds the product of all the previous ones by $1$). Prove that the differences of its neighbouring terms $(a_{n+1}-a_n)$ are squares of integers.

$2n$ teams take part in a football tournament ($n>1$). In each round the teams are divided into $n$ pairs, and the teams of each pair play each other. In this way $2n-1$ rounds were held, at the end of which each team had played each other team exactly once. A win gave $3$ points, a draw $1$, a loss $0$ points. It turned out that for each team the ratio of the points it had scored to the number of games it had played did not change after the last round. Prove that all the teams drew all their games.

The cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper are coloured black and white in a chessboard pattern. Let $X$ be a triangle of area $S$ with vertices at grid nodes. Show that there is a triangle similar to $X$ with vertices at grid nodes such that the area of its white part equals the area of its black part and equals $S$.

The emperor invited $2015$ wizards to a festival, some of whom are good and the rest evil. A good wizard always tells the truth, while an evil one may say anything. The wizards know who is good and who is evil, but the emperor does not.

At the festival the emperor asks each wizard (in the order he wishes) one question that can be answered "yes" or "no". Having questioned all the wizards, the emperor expels one of them. The expelled wizard goes out through an enchanted door, and the emperor learns whether he was good or evil. Then the emperor again asks each of the remaining wizards one question, again expels one, and so on, until the emperor decides to stop (he may do this after any question).

Prove that the emperor can expel all the evil wizards, removing at most one good one in the process.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. The altitude $AH$ and the median $CM$ are drawn. Denote their intersection point by $P$. The altitude drawn from the vertex $B$ of the triangle meets the perpendicular dropped from the point $H$ to the line $CM$ at the point $Q$. Prove that the lines $CQ$ and $BP$ are perpendicular.

Are there two polynomials with integer coefficients such that each of them has a coefficient whose absolute value is greater than $2015$, while all the coefficients of the product of these two polynomials have absolute values not exceeding $1$?
Can the number $\dfrac{1}{10}$ be represented as the product of ten positive proper fractions? (That is, of expressions of the form $\dfrac pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are natural numbers and $p<q$.)

Inside a convex quadrilateral $A_1A_2B_2B_1$ there is a point $C$ such that the triangles $CA_1A_2$ and $CB_1B_2$ are equilateral. The points $C_1$ and $C_2$ are symmetric to the point $C$ with respect to the lines $A_2B_2$ and $A_1B_1$ respectively. Prove that the triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_2B_2C_2$ are similar.

The equation with integer coefficients $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ has $4$ positive roots counted with multiplicity (that is, the sum of the multiplicities of all positive roots of this equation equals $4$). Find the smallest possible value of the coefficient $b$ under these conditions.

An infinite squared board is coloured in a chessboard pattern, and a non-zero integer is written in each white cell. After that, for each black cell the difference was computed: the product of the numbers in the cells adjacent to it horizontally minus the product of the numbers in the cells adjacent to it vertically. Can all such differences equal $1$?
$8$ non-intersecting balls (possibly of different sizes) are placed in a cube with edge $1$. Can the sum of the diameters of these balls be greater than $4$?

$2016$ teams took part in a single round-robin hockey tournament. According to the rules, a win gives $3$ points and a loss $0$ points, and in case of a draw overtime is played, whose winner gets $2$ points and the loser $1$ point. At the end of the tournament Ostap Bender was told the number of points scored by each team, on the basis of which he concluded that at least $N$ matches had ended in overtime. Find the largest possible value of $N$.

A quadratic trinomial $x^2+bx+c$ has two real roots. Each of its three coefficients (including the coefficient of $x^2$) was increased by $1$. Could it happen that both roots of the trinomial also increased by $1$?

All natural numbers greater than one were coloured in two colours, blue and red, so that the sum of any two blue numbers (including equal ones) is blue, and the product of any two red numbers (including equal ones) is red. It is known that both colours were used and that the number $1024$ was coloured blue. What colour could the number $2017$ have?

The point $O$ is the centre of the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $AOC$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ for the second time at the points $E$ and $F$. It turned out that the line $EF$ bisects the area of the triangle $ABC$. Find the angle $B$.

Vasya has a stone (homogeneous, without internal cavities) in the form of a convex polyhedron that has only triangular and hexagonal faces. Vasya claims that he has broken this stone into two parts from which a cube (without internal cavities) can be assembled. Can Vasya's words be true?
For which natural $n$ does there exist, for every natural $k\geqslant n$, a number with digit sum $k$ that is a multiple of $n$?

$36$ criminal gangs operate in Chicago, some of which are at enmity with each other. Each gangster belongs to several gangs, and any two gangsters belong to different sets of gangs. It is known that no gangster belongs to two gangs at enmity with each other. Moreover, it turned out that each gang to which some gangster does not belong is at enmity with some gang to which this gangster belongs. What is the largest number of gangsters there can be in Chicago?
Is there a number whose square contains in its decimal representation the sequence of digits "2018"?

In a squared square with side $2018$ some of the cells are coloured white and the rest black. It is known that one can cut out of this square a $10\times 10$ square all of whose cells are white, and a $10\times 10$ square all of whose cells are black. For what smallest $d$ can one guarantee that one can cut out of it a $10\times 10$ square in which the numbers of black and white cells differ by at most $d$?

The point $O$ is the centre of the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, and $AH$ is its altitude. The point $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the point $A$ to the line $CO$. Prove that the line $HP$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $AB$.

Call an arrangement of $n$ ones and $m$ zeros around a circle good if one can interchange a neighbouring zero and one in it so that an arrangement differing from the original one by a rotation is obtained. For which natural $m$ and $n$ does a good arrangement exist?

Carlson is eating a triangular cake. He cuts the cake along the bisector of one of its angles, chooses either of the two resulting parts and eats it, and repeats the same operation with the other part. If Carlson eats more than half of the cake, he will become a moderately well-fed man in the prime of life. Prove that sooner or later this will happen.

Prove that the number of ways to cut a $999\times 999$ square into three-cell L-shaped pieces (see the figure) is divisible by $2^7$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_2018_0_p6_fig.png

Give an example of a nine-digit natural number which is divisible by $2$ if its second digit (from the left) is crossed out, by $3$ if the third digit of the original number is crossed out, $\ldots$, by $9$ if the ninth digit of the original number is crossed out.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA'$ and $BB'$ are drawn. The point $O$ is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the distance from the point $A'$ to the line $BO$ equals the distance from the point $B'$ to the line $AO$.

$2019$ point grasshoppers sit on a line. In one move some grasshopper jumps over some other one so as to be at the same distance from it as before. Jumping only to the right, the grasshoppers can achieve that some two of them are at a distance of exactly $1$ mm from each other. Prove that the grasshoppers can achieve the same by jumping from the initial position only to the left.
Every point of the plane is coloured in one of three colours. Must there be a triangle of area $1$ all of whose vertices have the same colour?

Petya and Vasya play a game. For every five distinct variables from the set $x_1, \ldots, x_{10}$ there is a unique card on which their product is written. Petya and Vasya take cards in turn, Petya beginning. When all the cards have been taken, Vasya assigns values to the variables as he wishes, but so that $0\leqslant x_1\leqslant\ldots\leqslant x_{10}$. Can Vasya be sure to make the sum of the products on his cards greater than Petya's?

Consider on the squared plane the broken lines starting at the point $(0,0)$ with vertices at points with integer coordinates such that each successive segment goes along the sides of the cells either upwards or to the right. To each such broken line there corresponds a worm: the figure consisting of the cells of the plane that have at least one common point with this broken line. Prove that the number of worms that can be divided into two-cell dominoes in exactly $n>2$ different ways equals the number of natural numbers smaller than $n$ and coprime to $n$. (Worms are different if they consist of different sets of cells.)

Give an example of a quadratic trinomial $P(x)$ such that for every $x$ the equality
$$P(x)+P(x+1)+\cdots+P(x+10)=x^2$$
holds.

Among the spectators of a film festival there were equally many men and women. All the spectators liked the same number of films. Each film was liked by eight spectators. Prove that at least $3/7$ of the films have the following property: among the spectators who liked the film there are at least two men.
Is there a polygon with $19$ sides inscribed in a circle, no two of whose sides have equal lengths, and all of whose angles are expressed by an integer number of degrees?

The point $O$ is the centre of the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$. The perpendicular bisector of $BC$ meets $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $X$ and $Y$. The line $AO$ meets the line $BC$ at the point $D$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $ADM$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at a point $E$ different from $A$. Prove that the line $OE$ touches the circumcircle of the triangle $AXY$.

$1000$ consecutive integers are written on the board. In one move one may divide the written numbers into pairs arbitrarily and replace each pair of numbers by their sum and difference (it is not necessary to subtract the smaller from the larger; all the replacements happen simultaneously). Prove that $1000$ consecutive integers will never again appear on the board.

For which $k$ can one colour black several cells (a finite number, greater than zero) of the white squared plane so that on every vertical, horizontal and diagonal line of cells there are either exactly $k$ black cells or no black cells at all?

A natural number is written on the board. If its last digit (in the units place) is erased, a non-zero number remains which is divisible by $20$, and if its first digit is erased, a number divisible by $21$ remains. What is the smallest number that can be written on the board if its second digit is not $0$?
An isosceles trapezoid is given in which the sum of the lateral sides equals the larger base. Prove that the acute angle between the diagonals is not greater than $60^\circ$.

There is a squared strip, infinite in one direction, whose cells are numbered by the natural numbers, and a bag with ten stones. Initially there are no stones in the cells of the strip. One may do the following:

— move a stone from the bag to the first cell of the strip or back;

— if there is a stone in the cell with number $i$, one may move a stone from the bag to the cell with number $i+1$ or back.

Is it possible, acting according to these rules, to put a stone into the cell with number $1000$?

A point $P$ was taken inside a quadrilateral $ABCD$. The lines $BC$ and $AD$ meet at the point $X$. It turned out that the line $XP$ is the external bisector of the angles $APD$ and $BPC$. Let $PY$ and $PZ$ be the bisectors of the triangles $APB$ and $DPC$. Prove that the points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ lie on one line.

Let $p$ and $q$ be coprime natural numbers. A frog jumps along the number line, starting at the point $0$, each time either by $p$ to the right or by $q$ to the left. Once the frog returned to $0$. Prove that for every natural $d<p+q$ there are two numbers visited by the frog that differ by $d$.

The ceiling of a number $x$ is the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$. Prove that there is a real number $A$ such that for every natural $n$ the distance from the ceiling of $A^n$ to the nearest square of a natural number always equals $2$.
Find the largest natural number $n$ with the following property: for every odd prime $p$ smaller than $n$, the difference $n-p$ is also a prime number.

The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. The tangent $\ell$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at the point $A$ meets the line $BC$ at the point $K$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $MKN$ touches $\ell$.

Among any five nodes of ordinary squared paper there are necessarily two such that the midpoint of the segment between them is also a node of the squared paper. What is the smallest number of nodes of the grid of regular hexagons (see the figure) that one must take so that among them there are necessarily two such that the midpoint of the segment between them is also a node of this grid?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_2022_0_p3_fig.png
A polynomial of degree $2022$ with integer coefficients and leading coefficient $1$ is given. What is the largest number of roots it can have in the interval $(0,1)$?

Two triangles intersect in a hexagon which cuts off $6$ small triangles from them. The radii of the incircles of these six triangles are equal. Prove that the radii of the incircles of the two original triangles are also equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo10_2022_0_p5_fig.png

Andrei Mikhailovich wrote on the board all possible sequences of length $2022$ consisting of $1011$ zeros and $1011$ ones. Call two sequences compatible if they coincide in exactly $4$ positions. Prove that Andrei Mikhailovich can divide all the sequences into $20$ groups so that no two compatible sequences fall into the same group.

It is known about four integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ that
$$a+b+c+d=ab+bc+cd+da+1.$$
Prove that the absolute values of some two of these numbers differ by $1$.

Two teams of $20$ people each took part in the Moscow–Petushki relay race. Each of the teams divided the distance in its own way into $20$ not necessarily equal stages and distributed them among its members so that each ran exactly one stage (the speed of each runner is constant, but the speeds of different runners may differ). The first runners of both teams started simultaneously, and the baton is handed over instantly. What is the largest number of overtakings that could have occurred in such a race? Being ahead at a stage boundary does not count as an overtaking.

The perimeter of a triangle $ABC$ equals $1$. A circle $\omega$ touches the side $BC$, the extension of the side $AB$ at the point $P$ and the extension of the side $AC$ at the point $Q$. The line passing through the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ at the points $X$ and $Y$. Find the length of the segment $XY$.

The number $11\ldots1$ (with $900$ ones in all) is displayed on the screen of a supercomputer. Every second the supercomputer replaces it according to the following rule. The number is written in the form $\overline{AB}$, where $B$ consists of its last two digits, and is replaced by $2\cdot A+8\cdot B$ (if $B$ begins with a zero, the zero is omitted in the computation). For example, $305$ is replaced by $2\cdot3+8\cdot5=46$. If a number smaller than $100$ remains on the screen, the process stops. Is it true that it will stop?

Two circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ touching each other externally are given in the plane. A diameter $AB$ is chosen on the circle $\omega_1$, and a diameter $CD$ on the circle $\omega_2$. Consider all positions of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ for which $ABCD$ is a convex circumscribed quadrilateral, and let $I$ be the centre of its incircle. Find the locus of the points $I$.

Chameleons of $5$ colours live on an island. When one chameleon bites another, the colour of the bitten chameleon changes to one of these $5$ colours according to some rule, and the new colour depends only on the colour of the biter and the colour of the bitten one. It is known that $2023$ red chameleons can agree on a sequence of bites after which all of them become blue. For what smallest $k$ can one guarantee that $k$ red chameleons can agree so as to become blue?

For example, the rules may be as follows: if a red chameleon bites a green one, the bitten one changes its colour to blue; if a green one bites a red one, the bitten one stays red, that is, "changes its colour to red"; if a red chameleon bites a red one, the bitten one changes its colour to yellow, and so on. (The specific rules for changing colours may be arranged differently.)

Petya and Vasya play on the segment $[0,1]$, on which the points $0$ and $1$ are marked. The players move in turn, Petya beginning. In each move a player marks a point of the segment that has not been marked before. If after a player's move there are three consecutive segments between neighbouring marked points from which a triangle can be formed, the player who made this move is declared the winner, and the game ends. Can Petya be sure to win?
Prove that among the vertices of a convex nonagon one can find three that form an obtuse-angled triangle none of whose sides coincides with a side of the nonagon.

At the beginning of the year $n$ pairwise unacquainted schoolchildren joined a club of hypergraph lovers. During the year the club held $100$ meetings, and each meeting was attended by at least one schoolchild. Two schoolchildren became acquainted if there was at least one meeting that both of them attended. At the end of the year it turned out that the number of acquaintances of each schoolchild was not less than the number of meetings he attended. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which this could happen.

A circumscribed quadrilateral $ABCD$ with an obtuse angle $ABC$ is given. The rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at the point $P$, and the rays $DA$ and $CB$ at the point $Q$. Prove that $|AD-CD|\geqslant|r_1-r_2|$, where $r_1$ and $r_2$ are the radii of the incircles of the triangles $PBC$ and $QAB$.

Call a natural number $N$ strongly cubic if there is a monic cubic polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(f(f(N)))=0$, while $f(N)$ and $f(f(N))$ are not equal to $0$. Is it true that all numbers greater than $20^{24}$ are strongly cubic?

A real number is written on each of $99$ cards. All $99$ numbers are distinct, and their total sum is irrational. A stack of the $99$ cards is called unlucky if for every natural $k$ from $1$ to $99$ the sum of the numbers on the top $k$ cards is irrational. Petya computed in how many ways the original cards can be put into an unlucky stack. What is the smallest value he could have obtained?

Duke Summator chose some real numbers (at least one, but possibly infinitely many). Duke Subtractor did the same. It turned out that if $x$ is a number of Summator and $y$ a number of Subtractor, then $x+y$ is a number of Summator and $y-x$ is a number of Subtractor. Must all the numbers of Summator be numbers of Subtractor?

In a triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$ the altitude $CH$ is drawn. A circle passing through the points $C$ and $H$ meets the segments $AC$, $CB$ and $BH$ for the second time at the points $Q$, $P$ and $R$ respectively. The segments $HP$ and $CR$ meet at the point $T$. Which is greater: the area of the triangle $CPT$ or the sum of the areas of the triangles $CQH$ and $HTR$?

$100$ Knights of the Round Table arrived in Camelot; any two of them are either friends or enemies (friendship and enmity are mutual). The fairy Morgana can choose any knight and make him quarrel with all his friends and at the same time make friends with all his enemies. Morgana may cast this spell as many times as she likes. Prove that she can achieve that in the end there are two groups of $5$ knights such that each knight of the first group is at enmity with each knight of the second.

Are there natural numbers $m$ and $n$ and a polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(m)$ is not divisible by $n$, but $f(p^k)$ is divisible by $n$ for every prime number $p$ and every natural number $k$?

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $H$. The bisector of the angle $CBH$ meets the segment $CH$ at the point $X$, and the bisector of the angle $BCH$ meets the segment $BH$ at the point $Y$. Denote the angle $XA_1Y$ by $\alpha$. Define $\beta$ and $\gamma$ similarly. Find the value of the sum $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$.

$100$ elves, $100$ dwarves and $100$ orcs stand near a tavern. First $10$ elves, $10$ dwarves and $10$ orcs go into it. Then every minute one creature comes out of it and immediately another one goes in; after an elf comes out a dwarf always goes in, after a dwarf comes out an orc, and after an orc comes out an elf. Could it happen that by some moment every possible company of $30$ creatures had been in the tavern exactly once? All $300$ creatures are distinct.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. On its circumcircle the point $D$ diametrically opposite to the vertex $A$ is marked. Points $X$ and $Y$ on the side $BC$ are such that $BX=XD$ and $CY=YD$ (the point $X$ lies on the segment $BY$). Prove that $DA$ is the bisector of the angle $XDY$.

A quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ with non-zero integer coefficients $a$, $b$ and $c$ having an integer root is given. Can it happen that if any of these three coefficients is increased by $1$, the resulting equation remains quadratic and also has an integer root?

There are two hundred balls of a hundred colours, two balls of each colour. A magician has placed them arbitrarily into a hundred boxes, two balls per box; the player does not know what is where. In one move the player points at any two boxes, after which the magician, unnoticed by the player, chooses one ball from each of these boxes and interchanges them. If at some moment every box contains balls of different colours, the host gives the player a prize. Can the player act so as to be sure to get the prize, no matter how the magician interchanges the balls?

Points $D$ and $E$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ so that $BD=DE=CE$. On the segments $AB$, $AC$, $AE$ and $AD$ the points $L$, $K$, $P$ and $Q$ respectively are chosen (all the points $A, B, C, D, E, K, L, P, Q$ are distinct) so that
$$\angle EAD=\angle PDE=\angle QED=\angle AKP=\angle ALQ.$$
Prove that $LK+DE\leqslant AD+AE$.

Call a set of $k$ consecutive natural numbers good if one can choose for each of these numbers a prime divisor of it so that for any two different numbers different divisors are chosen. Otherwise call the set bad. Is it true that for every natural $k$ the number of bad sets of $k$ consecutive natural numbers is finite?

A natural number $n\geqslant 2$ is given. A symmetric polynomial $P(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is such that the equation $P(x_1, \ldots, x_n)=0$ has real solutions, and all these solutions are obtained by permuting the numbers of one single collection $a_1, \ldots, a_n$. It is known that this collection contains at least two different numbers. For each $n\geqslant 2$ find the smallest possible degree of the polynomial $P$.

A polynomial is called symmetric if it does not change under any permutation of its variables. The degree of a polynomial $P$ in several variables is the largest of the sums of the exponents of the variables in the non-zero terms (monomials) of the polynomial $P$ written in standard form. For example, the polynomial $P(x,y)=x^3y^3+xy^4+x^4y$ has degree $6$ (since $3+3=6$, and this is greater than $4+1=5$).
